Hi @zhuoweixinnengyan,

Before building anything, I’d settle a few things, because they decide whether the POC holds up.

On LangGraph: let n8n own the triggers, API calls, retries, dedupe and CRM sync. LangGraph is only worth adding for the loop where the outreach agent drafts, gets checked against your rules, and rewrites (cap it at two passes). I’d run that as a small Python service and call it from n8n over HTTP, so the exported workflow JSON still runs on its own and the graph can be versioned separately. If the loop turns out to be simple, n8n’s AI Agent node with a Structured Output Parser covers it with less to maintain. You’ll know which one after the first 50 leads.

On Apollo: people search doesn’t return emails or phone numbers. You search first, then make a separate enrichment call per person, and each enrichment spends credits. So filter hard before enriching (title, country, company size, and a dedupe against what’s already in your CRM). Search also stops at 50,000 records, so slice by region and segment instead of pulling one huge list. Run every address through Hunter’s verifier before a draft exists, and store the status on the lead.

For sodium-ion versus lithium-ion, I wouldn’t let the model guess fit in free text. The pitch lands differently by segment (cold climates, cost pressure, cycle life requirements), so have the research agent return a structured record: segment, likely use case, Na or Li fit, one specific reason, and the source. The outreach agent writes only from that record, and if a field is empty it leaves the line out. That’s what kills the invented “loved your recent project” openers.

Two guardrails for the POC. Drafts only, no auto-send: every lead lands in the CRM as pending review with the profile and draft attached. And a suppression list plus an unsubscribe line from day one, since you’re selling worldwide.

posts.name: Serhii Veselov
posts.cooked:
Hi,

Here is how I would structure it in n8n:

1. Workflow structure: split it into 3 workflows.

  • Onboarding: Google Sheets Trigger (new form response) → validation and normalization → create the user profile → generate the initial plan → send it via WhatsApp.

  • Daily: Schedule Trigger → load active users → Loop Over Items → generate the plan → send → log the result.

  • Inbound: WhatsApp Trigger → Switch (weight update, question, stop) → update the profile.

2. Form data: the Google Sheets Trigger or the Google Sheets node, then a Set/Edit Fields node to normalize types (age and weight as numbers, phone in E.164 format). Add an IF node for validation, for example an age range or a missing phone number.

3. Prompt: split it into a fixed system prompt (role, rules, safety limits, output format) and a dynamic user message (profile, goal, last 3-7 plans, yesterday’s progress). Ask for a structured JSON output (workout, meals, calories, protein, water), and validate it with the Structured Output Parser before sending.

4. Storage: for a prototype, Google Sheets works. Use one row per user and a separate tab for plan history and progress logs. For real usage, use Airtable or Postgres instead, because Sheets hits rate limits and gets slow.

5. WhatsApp: use the official WhatsApp Business Cloud API (Meta). Messages outside the 24-hour customer-service window require pre-approved templates, so plan the daily plan as a template. Check the current rules in Meta’s documentation.

6. A new plan every day: pass the previous plans into the prompt and instruct the model not to repeat exercises or meals. Adjust the load based on the progress data (weight, workouts completed).

7. Safety: enforce hard limits in the workflow logic, not only in the prompt. Set a minimum calorie floor, and block or flag users under 18, pregnant users, and users with medical conditions. Add a disclaimer that this is not medical advice, and offer a STOP option.

8. Reliability: add an Error Trigger workflow with an alert to Slack or Telegram, and retry settings on the LLM and WhatsApp nodes.

Start with the onboarding workflow and one test user, then add the daily schedule and progress tracking.

Happy to clarify any of these points here.

posts.cooked:
The part of this POC most teams underestimate isn’t the agent-building — it’s what happens after the agents write the emails: deliverability. A manufacturer domain that suddenly sends personalized B2B outreach needs SPF/DKIM/DMARC properly aligned and a warmup period, or the best lead list in the world lands in spam and the POC “fails” for reasons that have nothing to do with agent quality.

Worth deciding before the architecture: separate sending domain for the outbound system, ramp volumes gradually, and track bounce/reply rates from day one so the list quality question and the deliverability question don’t get conflated.

On the agent side, the pattern that’s worked for me in production: keep the research/enrichment/drafting agents as small single-responsibility stages with a deterministic review gate between “agent drafted” and “email goes out” — you get the personalization of agents with the auditability of a pipeline.

Hi,

The POC scope is well defined and the constraint that matters most is the one you

buried: official APIs only, no unauthorised scraping. That single rule decides the

architecture, so it is worth designing around it rather than fitting it in later.

What that means in practice. Most B2B lead-gen systems fail for the same reason:

they lean on scraped directories that dry up or get blocked, and the lead flow

quietly degrades. Restricting to official APIs changes the shape of the build:

- Discovery has to lean on legitimate structured sources and on enrichment

providers with real terms of service, not on page scraping.

- Enrichment and scoring become the core of the system, because you have fewer

leads and so each one has to be qualified harder before an agent spends effort

on it.

- The agent that writes outreach needs a factual guardrail. An agent that

invents a detail about a target company does more damage than no email at all,

so I would keep a strict split: the model composes, but every claim in the

email traces back to an enriched field that was actually retrieved.

Architecture I would propose for the POC:

- n8n as the orchestration spine, so the whole system is inspectable and you can

see and edit the flow, with each stage exportable as workflow JSON as you asked.

- LangGraph for the agentic parts where state and branching genuinely matter

(research, qualification, drafting), rather than forcing everything into one

loop.

- A CRM handoff at the end with status tracking, so nothing a lead-gen system

produces disappears into a mailbox.

- Manual review gate before send during the POC. Once the qualification and the

factual guardrail have proven themselves, it can go automatic. I would not open

that gate in week two.

On the sector: energy storage procurement and B2B supply chains are areas I

understand from the commercial side, which matters for judging whether a lead is

actually qualified rather than just well-formed. You can communicate in Chinese if

Here is how I would structure it in n8n:

1. Workflow structure: split it into 3 workflows.

  • Onboarding: Google Sheets Trigger (new form response) → validation and normalization → create the user profile → generate the initial plan → send it via WhatsApp.

  • Daily: Schedule Trigger → load active users → Loop Over Items → generate the plan → send → log the result.

  • Inbound: WhatsApp Trigger → Switch (weight update, question, stop) → update the profile.

2. Form data: the Google Sheets Trigger or the Google Sheets node, then a Set/Edit Fields node to normalize types (age and weight as numbers, phone in E.164 format). Add an IF node for validation, for example an age range or a missing phone number.

3. Prompt: split it into a fixed system prompt (role, rules, safety limits, output format) and a dynamic user message (profile, goal, last 3-7 plans, yesterday’s progress). Ask for a structured JSON output (workout, meals, calories, protein, water), and validate it with the Structured Output Parser before sending.

4. Storage: for a prototype, Google Sheets works. Use one row per user and a separate tab for plan history and progress logs. For real usage, use Airtable or Postgres instead, because Sheets hits rate limits and gets slow.

5. WhatsApp: use the official WhatsApp Business Cloud API (Meta). Messages outside the 24-hour customer-service window require pre-approved templates, so plan the daily plan as a template. Check the current rules in Meta’s documentation.

6. A new plan every day: pass the previous plans into the prompt and instruct the model not to repeat exercises or meals. Adjust the load based on the progress data (weight, workouts completed).

7. Safety: enforce hard limits in the workflow logic, not only in the prompt. Set a minimum calorie floor, and block or flag users under 18, pregnant users, and users with medical conditions. Add a disclaimer that this is not medical advice, and offer a STOP option.

8. Reliability: add an Error Trigger workflow with an alert to Slack or Telegram, and retry settings on the LLM and WhatsApp nodes.

Start with the onboarding workflow and one test user, then add the daily schedule and progress tracking.

The part of this POC most teams underestimate isn’t the agent-building — it’s what happens after the agents write the emails: deliverability. A manufacturer domain that suddenly sends personalized B2B outreach needs SPF/DKIM/DMARC properly aligned and a warmup period, or the best lead list in the world lands in spam and the POC “fails” for reasons that have nothing to do with agent quality.

Worth deciding before the architecture: separate sending domain for the outbound system, ramp volumes gradually, and track bounce/reply rates from day one so the list quality question and the deliverability question don’t get conflated.

- Discovery has to lean on legitimate structured sources and on enrichment

- n8n as the orchestration spine, so the whole system is inspectable and you can

- A CRM handoff at the end with status tracking, so nothing a lead-gen system

comments.author: abdullah30
comments.text:
Hi  @zhuoweixinnengyan , 
 Before building anything, I’d settle a few things, because they decide whether the POC holds up. 
 On LangGraph: let n8n own the triggers, API calls, retries, dedupe and CRM sync. LangGraph is only worth adding for the loop where the outreach agent drafts, gets checked against your rules, and rewrites (cap it at two passes). I’d run that as a small Python service and call it from n8n over HTTP, so the exported workflow JSON still runs on its own and the graph can be versioned separately. If the loop turns out to be simple, n8n’s AI Agent node with a Structured Output Parser covers it with less to maintain. You’ll know which one after the first 50 leads. 
 On Apollo: people search doesn’t return emails or phone numbers. You search first, then make a separate enrichment call per person, and each enrichment spends credits. So filter hard before enriching (title, country, company size, and a dedupe against what’s already in your CRM). Search also stops at 50,000 records, so slice by region and segment instead of pulling one huge list. Run every address through Hunter’s verifier before a draft exists, and store the status on the lead. 
 For sodium-ion versus lithium-ion, I wouldn’t let the model guess fit in free text. The pitch lands differently by segment (cold climates, cost pressure, cycle life requirements), so have the research agent return a structured record: segment, likely use case, Na or Li fit, one specific reason, and the source. The outreach agent writes only from that record, and if a field is empty it leaves the line out. That’s what kills the invented “loved your recent project” openers. 
 Two guardrails for the POC. Drafts only, no auto-send: every lead lands in the CRM as pending review with the profile and draft attached. And a suppression list plus an unsubscribe line from day one, since you’re selling worldwide. 
 I’m sending you a DM with a few past builds.

comments.author: Serhii_Veselov
comments.text:
Hi, 
 Here is how I would structure it in n8n: 
 1. Workflow structure: split it into 3 workflows. 
 
 
 Onboarding: Google Sheets Trigger (new form response) → validation and normalization → create the user profile → generate the initial plan → send it via WhatsApp. 
 
 
 Daily: Schedule Trigger → load active users → Loop Over Items → generate the plan → send → log the result. 
 
 
 Inbound: WhatsApp Trigger → Switch (weight update, question, stop) → update the profile. 
 
 
 2. Form data: the Google Sheets Trigger or the Google Sheets node, then a Set/Edit Fields node to normalize types (age and weight as numbers, phone in E.164 format). Add an IF node for validation, for example an age range or a missing phone number. 
 3. Prompt: split it into a fixed system prompt (role, rules, safety limits, output format) and a dynamic user message (profile, goal, last 3-7 plans, yesterday’s progress). Ask for a structured JSON output (workout, meals, calories, protein, water), and validate it with the Structured Output Parser before sending. 
 4. Storage: for a prototype, Google Sheets works. Use one row per user and a separate tab for plan history and progress logs. For real usage, use Airtable or Postgres instead, because Sheets hits rate limits and gets slow. 
 5. WhatsApp: use the official WhatsApp Business Cloud API (Meta). Messages outside the 24-hour customer-service window require pre-approved templates, so plan the daily plan as a template. Check the current rules in Meta’s documentation. 
 6. A new plan every day: pass the previous plans into the prompt and instruct the model not to repeat exercises or meals. Adjust the load based on the progress data (weight, workouts completed). 
 7. Safety: enforce hard limits in the workflow logic, not only in the prompt. Set a minimum calorie floor, and block or flag users under 18, pregnant users, and users with medical conditions. Add a disclaimer that this is not medical advice, and offer a STOP option. 
 8. Reliability: add an Error Trigger workflow with an alert to Slack or Telegram, and retry settings on the LLM and WhatsApp nodes. 
 Start with the onboarding workflow and one test user, then add the daily schedule and progress tracking. 
 Happy to clarify any of these points here.

The part of this POC most teams underestimate isn’t the agent-building — it’s what happens after the agents write the emails: deliverability. A manufacturer domain that suddenly sends personalized B2B outreach needs SPF/DKIM/DMARC properly aligned and a warmup period, or the best lead list in the world lands in spam and the POC “fails” for reasons that have nothing to do with agent quality. 
 Worth deciding before the architecture: separate sending domain for the outbound system, ramp volumes gradually, and track bounce/reply rates from day one so the list quality question and the deliverability question don’t get conflated. 
 On the agent side, the pattern that’s worked for me in production: keep the research/enrichment/drafting agents as small single-responsibility stages with a deterministic review gate between “agent drafted” and “email goes out” — you get the personalization of agents with the auditability of a pipeline.

Hi, 
 The POC scope is well defined and the constraint that matters most is the one you 
 buried: official APIs only, no unauthorised scraping. That single rule decides the 
 architecture, so it is worth designing around it rather than fitting it in later. 
 What that means in practice. Most B2B lead-gen systems fail for the same reason: 
 they lean on scraped directories that dry up or get blocked, and the lead flow 
 quietly degrades. Restricting to official APIs changes the shape of the build: 
 - Discovery has to lean on legitimate structured sources and on enrichment 
 providers with real terms of service, not on page scraping. 
 - Enrichment and scoring become the core of the system, because you have fewer 
 leads and so each one has to be qualified harder before an agent spends effort 
 on it. 
 - The agent that writes outreach needs a factual guardrail. An agent that 
 invents a detail about a target company does more damage than no email at all, 
 so I would keep a strict split: the model composes, but every claim in the 
 email traces back to an enriched field that was actually retrieved. 
 Architecture I would propose for the POC: 
 - n8n as the orchestration spine, so the whole system is inspectable and you can 
 see and edit the flow, with each stage exportable as workflow JSON as you asked. 
 - LangGraph for the agentic parts where state and branching genuinely matter 
 (research, qualification, drafting), rather than forcing everything into one 
 loop. 
 - A CRM handoff at the end with status tracking, so nothing a lead-gen system 
 produces disappears into a mailbox. 
 - Manual review gate before send during the POC. Once the qualification and the 
 factual guardrail have proven themselves, it can go automatic. I would not open 
 that gate in week two. 
 On the sector: energy storage procurement and B2B supply chains are areas I 
 understand from the commercial side, which matters for judging whether a lead is 
 actually qualified rather than just well-formed. You can communicate in Chinese if 
 that is easier at any point. 
 For the POC I would suggest we agree the two or three target customer profiles 
 before any code, since the qualification logic depends entirely on them. 
 Happy to share a comparable agent system I have built.

@zhuoweixinnengyan  Hello, I hope you see this. I took some time to think through how to structure the POC so it stays useful for your sales team instead of creating extra cleanup later. 
 The main risks on a 2-4 week energy-storage lead system are usually these three: 
 
 The list fills with the wrong buyers (resellers, consumers, or competitors). Keep the first filter in plain rules (region, buyer type, Na/Li fit) before any research agent runs. Dedupe on domain against your CRM. Low-confidence leads go to a review queue, not to email. 
 The writer invents a fact about the prospect. Every claim in the draft must cite a URL from the research step. Anything without a source is removed. Nothing is sent until someone on your side approves it in the CRM. The POC stays on drafts only. 
 Official API limits or bounces stop the run or hurt the domain. Rate-limit and retry every call. Verify emails before drafting. Cap daily sends. Alert on failures and bounce spikes. 
 
 n8n handles the reliable parts: pull from official sources, filter, dedupe, rate-limit, and write to the CRM. The research and writer step only runs on leads that already passed. That keeps the work inside the 2-4 weeks and gives you a list you can actually use. 
 Full disclosure: I am with Pond AI, we build custom AI agents. If you want this mapped against your CRM and the official sources before the POC starts, we can do the architecture for free. You keep the map even if you hire someone else, and there’s a 7-day refund if you get it built with us.
